text: A fraud detector flags a transaction. It catches 95 percent of real fraud and only raises a false alarm on 2 percent of legitimate transactions. Surely, when it flags something, it's very likely fraud? Most people guess around 95 percent. The real answer is about 19 percent. Bayes' theorem explains why, and it turns how likely is this evidence if the hypothesis were true into how likely is the hypothesis, now that I've seen the evidence.

From the definition of conditional probability, rearranging gives Bayes' theorem: P of H given E equals P of E given H, times P of H, divided by P of E. The prior, P of H, is how likely the hypothesis was before the evidence — for fraud, that's the base rate. The likelihood is how likely the evidence is if H is true. The posterior, P of H given E, is the updated belief we actually want.

Assume 0.5 percent of transactions are fraud, the detector flags 95 percent of real fraud, and it flags 2 percent of legitimate transactions. Plugging into the formula: overall, 2.465 percent of transactions get flagged, but only about 19.3 percent of flagged transactions are actually fraud. The other roughly 81 percent are false alarms.

Percentages are slippery — counts are easier. Imagine 100,000 transactions: 500 are fraud, and the detector catches 475 of them. 99,500 are legitimate, and the detector still flags 1,990 of them. Total flagged is 2,465, and the truly-fraud fraction is 475 over 2,465, about 19.3 percent. Even a tiny 2 percent false positive rate, applied to a huge legitimate majority, produces four times more false alarms than true catches — the base rate fallacy.

When the formula feels abstract, simulate the world and count. Across 2 million simulated transactions, flagging fraud 95 percent of the time and legitimate transactions 2 percent of the time, the fraction of flagged transactions that were truly fraud came out at 0.1921 — close to the exact 0.1927, the small gap just simulation noise.

Holding the detector fixed and changing only the base rate: at a 0.1 percent prior, the posterior is just 4.5 percent. At 0.5 percent, it's 19.3. At 5 percent, 71.4. At 20 percent, 92.2. The exact same detector is nearly useless on very rare events and quite strong on common ones — which is why judging a classifier by accuracy alone can be misleading when classes are imbalanced.

Bayes' theorem chains — yesterday's posterior becomes today's prior. If a second, independent alert flags the same transaction, feed 0.1927 back in as the new prior, and the probability of fraud jumps to about 92 percent. A caveat: this assumes the two alerts are truly independent given the real status. If both look at the same underlying features, their errors are correlated, and the real posterior would be lower.

Recall the plan-and-churn table from last lesson: P of churn given Free was 0.3, P of Free was 0.5, P of churn was 0.2. Bayes gives P of Free given churn as 0.3 times 0.5 divided by 0.2, equals 0.75 — exactly the 150-of-200 we counted directly. Bayes' theorem is the bridge between the two directions of any conditional.

The Naive Bayes classifier applies this formula with many features at once, and an entire approach called Bayesian statistics treats model parameters themselves as having priors and posteriors. To recap: always ask for the base rate — a strong test on a rare event still produces mostly false positives. Natural frequencies and simulation make the result concrete. Next, we move from events to numbers: random variables and expected value.
